Then send them to Sao Paulo, which nobody visits for the beaches, and to a state whose economy depends on one commodity. They will stop romanticizing it in a week.

This is the last of three reports from Brazil, and it begins with a number that surprised me. Around seventy percent of the electricity here comes from renewable sources, which is a figure most European countries would like to have and very few visitors ever hear about. That is not the country people describe to me before I fly. What they describe is either a beach or a crisis, and Brazil spends a great deal of its energy correcting both pictures at the same time. I spent a week in Sao Paulo, a city of twelve million people where the traffic is famous and the concert halls are not, and then four days in the northeast, where the infrastructure gets thinner and the welcome does not. If there is one thing I am taking home, it is this. Nobody I met simplified their own country for me. They complicated it, patiently, until I understood.

Here is the trap, and almost everybody at the table falls into it. Somebody asks you about your country, and you have about two seconds to choose between defending it and apologizing for it, and both of those are losing moves. There is a third option, and it is easier in English than people think. Give one fact, then one qualification, then stop talking. Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America, which sounds better than it feels from the inside. The public health system covers two hundred million people, though the wait for an appointment can be six months. Notice what happens there. You have not defended anything and you have not run your own country down. You have made the person opposite you curious, which is the only outcome that keeps a conversation alive. And the second half of every one of those sentences is a relative clause. That is all it is.
